name: Iris Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out on a second-hand e-bike by eleven, doing food for the lunch rush round the old town and the university. Afternoons I take small parcels from the depot by the ring road if the parcel app offers any. Evenings are food again until about ten. I still get lost in the new estates behind the hospital, and my rating sits at 4.6, which the app treats like a crime.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside and nobody standing over me. I like the cook at the noodle place on Mill Street who always gives me a spring roll. What wears me out is the pay changing without warning, the rain, and hills with a dead battery. Last month the base fee per drop went down again and nobody explained why. I share a flat above a laundrette with my friend Dana, and most months I have maybe two weeks of rent put by, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at the depot was scared of robots and it turns out the problem is the same as always: the apps paying us less. I'd post that the fight is about fees, not about some clever computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing gets better. The danger was never AI for me, it was the app deciding I'm worth a bit less each month. If nothing radical changes, I'm still one bad week away from asking Dana to cover my half of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding, same hours, same streets. I'd go to the riders' meeting at the community hall that a couple of the lads keep talking about, because if we don't push on fees nobody will. I'd try to get the bike paid off by spring so that's one less bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. Nothing changing with AI is like being told the storm missed you, but your roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay already changes without warning. Where would you be a year from now, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same, honestly, maybe worse if more people sign up because other jobs are scarce round here. There aren't many other delivery firms in town, so I can't just switch. I'd still be doing lunch and dinner and hoping for a good Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about the fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The riders' group, and I'd sign the petition to the council about minimum pay for app work. I don't trust the app's support chat at all. It's a script that says sorry and changes nothing.

say: **AI was never** the real threat to riders; the app cutting our fees is.
We should be organising about **pay per drop**, not panicking about robots.
think: Nothing changing means I stay **one bad week** from not making rent.
The app already decides my worth, and it **lowers it** a bit every month.
do: Keep riding the **same lunch and dinner** shifts round the old town.
Go to the **riders' meeting** at the community hall and sign the council petition.
Pay off the **e-bike loan** by spring to remove one monthly bill.
feel: **Tired** rather than frightened, because the old money worries never left.
S0.quote: Nothing changing with AI is like being told the storm missed you, but your roof was already leaking.
fieldNote: Her worry in the calm world is **money**, not technology; fee cuts already squeeze her.
Strong **pro-organising** instinct, but she distrusts anything the app offers, including its support chat.
Few other delivery firms in town leaves her **no easy switch**.

steps.text: Keep the lunch and dinner food shifts around the old town
Join the riders' group meeting at the community hall
Clear the e-bike loan by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say watch the apps, because that's where the change hits us first. If AI is doing the booking and the customer messages, it'll also be doing our pay and our ratings even harder. I'd tell people to back the riders' group before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my legs are safe for now, but the boss in my pocket gets smarter. The app will squeeze routes tighter and punish me for every wrong turn in those estates. And if office people lose jobs, half of them will sign up to deliver, and there's only so many orders in a town this size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to use any of the AI route helpers, because I don't trust where that data goes. I'd go to every riders' meeting and help hand out leaflets at the depot. I'd ask the noodle place on Mill Street if they want a direct rider a few nights a week, off the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cornered. Not falling yet, but the walls get a bit closer every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots spread slowly. Does the thinking AI part touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, through the app. It already decides who gets the good drops, and if it gets better at that, slow riders like me get the scraps. The customers' messages would be answered by a bot, so when a complaint comes in, there's no human to explain the lift was broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then takeaway coffee, then I'd stop sending money for my mum's birthday present, which I'd hate. After that it's the phone contract, and I can't work without the phone.

say: The change hits riders through the **app**, which will run our pay and ratings even harder.
Everyone should back the **riders' group** before the new rules settle in.
think: My legs are safe for now, but the **app boss** in my pocket gets stricter.
Laid-off office workers signing up would mean **more riders** chasing the same orders.
do: Refuse the app's **AI route helpers** because she doesn't trust the data use.
Hand out **leaflets** at the depot and attend every riders' meeting.
Ask the Mill Street **noodle place** about direct deliveries off the app.
feel: Resentful that a **bot** would judge her without hearing her side.
S1.quote: My legs are safe for now, but the boss in my pocket gets smarter.
fieldNote: She sees the **app as the boss**, so thinking AI reaches her through management, not through her own tasks.
Resistant to tools yet **active politically**; her energy goes into organising, not learning.
Fear of **new riders** flooding a small town market is concrete and specific.

steps.text: Hand out riders' group leaflets at the parcel depot
Offer the Mill Street noodle place direct evening deliveries
Cancel the gym and takeaway coffees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, with a basic income or at least proper pay for whoever's left. I'd be loud about it, posting, marching, the lot. Nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apps would be run by AGI from day one, so pay and orders get even sharper. Carrying a bag up some stairs is all I've got, and the robots would be doing that by 2031. I haven't got a trade, I haven't got savings, and I'm not good with tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride as many hours as my body takes in those three years and try to save anything at all. I'd join the riders' union properly and go to the protests in the city. I'd probably move in with my mum to stop paying rent, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for the bus that runs you over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do with that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, mostly, and fight. Three years sounds like time but on my pay it's maybe a couple of months of rent saved at best. I'd want the union to win something written down, like a fund for riders the robots replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmate Dana to start looking for someone else to share with, because I might not be able to stay. She'd say don't be daft, but she works in a call centre, so the thinking AI gets her first, two years before the robots get me.

say: The **government must** step in with a basic income or proper pay for whoever's left.
Nobody **voted** for this, and I'd say so loudly at marches and online.
think: The app gets **sharper** in 2028, then the robots end my job around **2031**.
I have **no trade**, no savings and little confidence with technology.
do: Ride **maximum hours** for three years and save whatever is left.
Join the **riders' union** properly and travel to protests in the city.
Move back in with **her mum** to stop paying rent.
feel: **Sick** and dreading something she can see coming.
S2.quote: Carrying a bag up some stairs is all I've got, and the robots would be doing that by 2031.
fieldNote: She understands the **three-year gap** but thinks her pay can't turn it into real savings.
Her flatmate's **call centre job** falls first, so the household loses twice.
Moving home to her mum is a **painful fallback** she names reluctantly.

steps.text: Sign up as a full member of the riders' union
Join city protests calling for a basic income
Bank every spare pound from extra evening shifts
Move back into her mum's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: we need rules and a safety net, and we need them written now, not after. I'd say five years is enough time for politicians to act if they actually wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a slower countdown but the same ending. The robots would come round 2034, so I'd be about 35. That's young enough to start again, but starting again from nothing on a rider's pay is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at the care course at the college, because looking after people feels like the last thing a robot should do. I'd keep riding to pay for it. I'd stay with the union and push for the retraining money to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe a bit. Five years is long enough to try something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years enough time to learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it's evenings and free. My cousin did the care course and now works in a home. My cousin says care work pays rubbish but steady, and rubbish and steady sounds better than rubbish and vanishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if it was for something like a course, and not for the app. I'd still not let it plan my routes. But I'm not stupid, if everyone is using it in five years, I'd have to learn the basics.

say: **Five years** is enough for politicians to act, if they actually want to.
Rules and a **safety net** need to be written now, not after the robots arrive.
think: The robots come around **2034**, when I'd be about 35.
Starting again **from nothing** on a rider's pay is the hard part.
do: Enrol in the evening **care course** at the local college.
Keep **riding** to pay for the course.
Push the union to make **retraining money** real.
feel: Still **uneasy**, but able to breathe a bit with five years to plan.
S3.quote: My cousin says care work pays rubbish but steady, and rubbish and steady sounds better than rubbish and vanishing.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from pure protest towards **retraining** in care work.
Her cousin's experience is the **proof** she needs before changing course.
She shifts slightly on **AI tools**, but only for study, never for the app.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening care course at the local college
Keep riding food shifts to pay course costs
Press the riders' union for real retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. Workers should use it to organise and get the rules right, not wait for the companies to be kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably still drag my feet for the first few years. That's me, I don't like change. But ten years means I could do the care course, work part-time, and not be on the bike at 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride for another year or two and save what I can. Then I'd do the care course and try to get on at the home where my cousin works. I'd keep paying union dues the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. The bike and the money are still the same problems they are now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to be doing at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working in a care home, with a contract and a rota I can plan around. Maybe living with someone, maybe not with Dana. Not watching a fee notice pop up every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the app squeezes me all the way there. Ten years is long, but rent is every month, and the delivery app is cutting fees now, not in 2036.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and workers should use it to organise.
Getting the **rules right** can't depend on companies being kind.
think: I'd probably **drag my feet** for the first few years.
The **care course** and part-time work could get me off the bike by 37.
do: Ride and **save** for one or two more years.
Take the **care course** and apply at her cousin's care home.
Keep paying **union dues** the whole decade.
feel: **Calmer**, but still weighed down by today's fees and rent.
S4.quote: Ten years is long, but rent is every month, and the delivery app is cutting fees now, not in 2036.
fieldNote: Long warning helps her **plan**, but current fee cuts keep her mood anxious.
She admits her own **slowness to change**, which is honest and self-aware.
Her goal is a **contract and a rota**, not more money.

steps.text: Save from riding for another two years
Train in care work and apply at her cousin's care home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years is nothing on my money. What would help is a law that sets a floor on pay per hour for app riders, and real money for retraining that doesn't need me to quit work first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Most of them are lovely. If a robot brings the curry, nobody checks on the old man on Tanner Lane who only orders so someone knocks on his door. I'd miss that, and so would he.

headlineQuote: If a robot brings the curry, nobody checks on the old man on Tanner Lane who only orders so someone knocks on his door.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** e-bike rider doing food and small parcels in a small town, with under a month of rent saved.
She treats the **app as her boss** and resents its unexplained fee cuts more than any robot.
She avoids **AI tools** and new tech, but puts her energy into the riders' group and union.
With more warning she leans towards a **care course**, following her cousin into a care home.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years of rider pay can't build any real cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A legal **pay floor** for app riders and **retraining money** that doesn't require quitting first.
